title: Prenatal developmental toxicity of the 70% ethanolic extract of defatted Lepidium sativum L. seeds in Wistar rats
content:
by Teshome Gebremeskel Aragie, Kaleab Asres, Wondwosen Ergete, Samual Woldekidan, Abiy Abebe, Bihonegn Sisay, Girma Seyoum

Introduction

Lepidium sativum Linn. seeds are widely consumed for medicinal and nutritional purposes, including among pregnant women; however, its safety profile during gestation remains inadequately defined. Therefore, this study evaluated the prenatal developmental toxicity of Lepidium sativum seeds in rats.

Methods

A total of five groups of pregnant Wistar rats were employed to evaluate the prenatal developmental effects of Lepidium sativum seed extract in two independent experimental arms. Treatments were administered via oral gavage during critical period of organogenesis (gestational day 12 [GD12] with the aim to evaluate the extract’s effect on embryonic development. In GD12 experiment, each group containing a specific number of rats: group I and V consisted of ten rats each, while groups II, III, and IV included nine rats per group. Separate cohorts were examined on GD20 to capture near term developmental outcomes and late-stage developmental effects of the extract. The number of pregnant rats available for GD20 subgroup was ten in groups I, IV, and V, nine in group II, and seven in group III respectively. In both studies, groups I- III served as experimental groups and were given 250 mg/kg, 500 mg/kg, and 1000 mg/kg of the extract respectively during GD6–12. While, groups IV and V were pair-fed and ad libitum controls respectively. One-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test was used to compare the groups, and statistical significance was declared at p < 0.05.

Results

In the GD12 subgroup, embryos from 1000 mg/kg of the extract exhibited significantly lower morphological scores in the embryonic heart (p < 0.01), otic (p = 0.002), and olfactory (p = 0.004) systems. A higher incidence of stillbirths and low birthweight pups was observed in 1000 mg/kg treated rats of GD20. Additionally, brain ventricular dilation was observed in 8% of fetuses from groups treated with 1000 mg/kg compared to the controls (p < 0.001).

Conclusions

Oral administration of Lepidium sativum seed extract during gestational day 6–12 at 500 mg/kg and 1000 mg/kg doses was associated with significant developmental delays in rat embryos. The extract also resulted in a higher number of stillbirths, low birthweight, and developmental delays in rat fetuses.
